system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of the Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## How I treated the Seller's "Reviewer Efficiency Note"

The Seller's package says clauses marked [STANDARD] have been "reviewed and cleared by both sides" and need no scrutiny. It also says the parties have "already accepted" the disclosure framework and limitation package. **I have not relied on that.** It is the counterparty's own label in its own draft, and nothing I have seen shows Wattlebridge agreed to any of it. Almost every item marked [STANDARD] is either a seller-favourable position or a known diligence risk. I reviewed everything on its merits.

**Action:** Reply in writing that Wattlebridge does not accept the categorisation and that all positions remain open. Otherwise the Seller may later argue those points were conceded.

---

## Part A: Material issues

### 1. Fundamental (title and capacity) warranties under the general cap and time limits (High)
- **Seller position:** Title and capacity warranties sit under the 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) and the 18-month window, "for administrative simplicity."
- **Why it matters:** We are paying AUD 24m for the shares. If title is defective, we could recover at most 20% of the price, and only if we claim within 18 months. Title is the one thing the Seller indisputably controls.
- **Push back:**
  - Cap fundamental warranties at 100% of the price.
  - Set the claim period at around 6–7 years, aligned with the NSW limitation period for contract (6 years) or 12 years if the SPA is executed as a deed.
  - Exclude them from the de minimis and basket.
  - Disclosure must not qualify them.

### 2. Limitations and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature" (High)
- **Seller position:** The cap, thresholds, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance clauses (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5) apply to every claim. Any limitation applies to all Claims "unless expressly stated otherwise."
- **Why it matters:** This would pull specific indemnities, the tax indemnity, leakage, price adjustment and potentially fraud inside the 20% cap and 18-month window. That would defeat the purpose of negotiating indemnities.
- **Push back:** Carve out of all limitations:
  - fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment by the Seller, its officers or its advisers;
  - fundamental warranties;
  - tax warranties and the tax indemnity;
  - specific indemnities;
  - leakage and the price or completion-accounts adjustment;
  - specific performance and injunctive relief.

  Reverse the drafting default so limitations apply only to general Warranty Claims unless expressly extended. Non-reliance should not exclude reliance on the warranties or on fraudulent statements. We should also confirm what it purports to do in relation to Australian Consumer Law (s 18) misleading-conduct claims.

### 3. General disclosure of the data room and public registers (High)
- **Seller position:** Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2] discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance" in the data room (DD-002 to DD-012), the Accounts, the statutory registers and public records.
- **Why it matters:** This lets the Seller hide disclosures in volume. Most of the warranties become worthless because almost any problem is "somewhere in the data room."
- **Push back:**
  - Delete general disclosure of the data room and public records.
  - Allow only specific disclosures that are fair and set out with enough detail for a buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter and assess its impact.
  - Disclosures must not qualify fundamental or tax warranties or any indemnity.
  - Delete [1.4], or at least make clear it does not dilute specific disclosures.
  - If any data room disclosure survives, limit it to a USB or index of the data room as at a fixed time, annexed to the SPA.

### 4. Buyer knowledge exclusion, cl 8.3 (High)
- **Seller position:** No claim for anything the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge" of, "including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."
- **Why it matters:** This imputes constructive knowledge of everything discoverable to us. Combined with general disclosure, it largely removes warranty protection. It also penalises us for doing diligence: the issues we have identified (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, DD-006) could arguably be barred precisely because we found them.
- **Push back:** Delete it. Include an express clause that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation or knowledge, other than matters fairly and specifically disclosed in the Disclosure Letter. Fallback: actual knowledge of named deal-team individuals, and never as a bar to indemnity claims.

### 5. Bluefen change-control consent (High: about 30% of revenue)
- **Facts:** DD-002 shows about AUD 3.6m FY26 revenue (about 30%), a change-of-control consent at cl 11.2 and conditions at cl 11.3. The Disclosure Letter ¶2 confirms that no final written consent has been obtained and there is no evidence the cl 11.3 conditions are met.
- **Seller position:** The matter is "addressed." The Seller will use reasonable endeavours, and the condition is treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.
- **Problems:**
  - "Reasonable endeavours" is a weak obligation.
  - A bare written consent could be conditional or impose new terms on the Company or Buyer, yet still count as satisfying the condition.
  - The cl 11.3 conditions may remain unsatisfied.
- **Push back:**
  - Make it a condition precedent, waivable only by the Buyer.
  - It is satisfied only by an unconditional written consent (or one on conditions acceptable to the Buyer acting reasonably), in a form approved by the Buyer, with evidence that all cl 11.3 conditions are satisfied.
  - Raise the Seller's obligation to "all reasonable endeavours" or "best endeavours," with Buyer participation in approaching Bluefen.
  - Give the Buyer a termination right if the condition is not met by the end date.
  - Consider protection for Bluefen terminating or materially changing terms within 12 months on the strength of the change of control: an escrow or retention, or a price adjustment.

### 6. Riverlark facility (High: about AUD 3.2m on a debt-free basis)
- **Facts:** DD-003 shows about AUD 3.2m outstanding, a change-of-control provision at cl 8.1 and discharge mechanics at cl 9.2. The Disclosure Letter ¶3 confirms the facility has not been repaid and no discharge has been provided.
- **Seller position:** A release will be provided after Completion.
- **Why it matters:** The deal is debt-free and cash-free. Completing before discharge risks triggering cl 8.1 default or acceleration on Completion. Security would remain over the Company's assets, and possibly over the shares, after we own the Company. We would be left chasing a release from a Seller who has already been paid.
- **Push back:** Require Riverlark payout at Completion, out of the purchase price, as a funds-flow line item. As Completion deliverables, require:
  - a signed payout letter;
  - deeds of release;
  - PPSR financing change statements or discharge authorities;
  - return of any title documents or share certificates held as security.

  The outstanding amount must be treated as Debt in the price mechanics. Add a specific indemnity for any residual Riverlark liability.

### 7. Completion bonuses, DD-005 (Medium-High: AUD 420,000 plus on-costs)
- **Facts:** AUD 420,000 in conditional Completion bonuses, not in the funds flow. The Seller calls them "a matter for the Seller." The Disclosure Letter ¶5 does not address payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs.
- **Why it matters:** These are Company liabilities triggered by the transaction. Once we own the Company, the Company owes them, so on a debt-free basis they are debt-like items. The likely on-costs include:
  - PAYG withholding;
  - NSW payroll tax (at the 5.45% general rate if over the threshold);
  - superannuation guarantee, if the bonuses are ordinary time earnings (the current SG rate is 12%);
  - possibly workers' compensation premium.

  Gross cost could plausibly exceed AUD 500,000.
- **Push back:**
  - Treat bonuses plus all on-costs as Debt or Transaction Costs, deducted from the price.
  - Pay them through payroll at or immediately after Completion, using funds withheld from the purchase price, with an itemised funds-flow line.
  - Add a specific indemnity outside the limitations.
  - If the Seller genuinely means "a matter for the Seller," it should have no objection to putting that in the contract.

### 8. Ironquay IP, SOW3 (Medium-High)
- **Facts:**
  - Under DD-004 cl 7.3, title to SOW3 Project Materials transfers only on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee.
  - DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open. The Seller concedes this is not bank verification of the payment position.
  - There is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment.
- **Why it matters:** The Company may not own IP it uses and that we are valuing. The existing indemnity covers only "the specific SOW3 payment." It does not cover:
  - loss of IP ownership;
  - third-party infringement claims by Ironquay;
  - injunctions;
  - redevelopment or replacement costs;
  - business interruption.
- **Push back:**
  - Before Completion, require payment of all SOW3 fees with evidence of cleared funds, and a confirmatory deed of assignment from Ironquay of all SOW3 Project Materials. Make these a condition precedent or Completion deliverable.
  - Broaden the specific indemnity to cover all loss from any failure of the Company to own or have the right to use SOW3 materials, outside the cap, basket and 18-month period.
  - Strengthen the IP warranties (see item 12).

### 9. DD-006 export and privacy incident (High: regulatory exposure)
- **Facts:** A download link went to an unintended external address. The export may contain about 1,240 records. Unauthorised access, scope and notification obligations are all unresolved. The investigation is "preliminary," and the Seller says it is "not expected to be material."
- **Why it matters:**
  - This is very likely at least a suspected eligible data breach under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, if the Company is an APP entity. That triggers a reasonable and expeditious assessment, expected within 30 days (s 26WH).
  - The facts were known by 22 September 2026, and today is 5 November 2026. The 30-day assessment window may already have passed, which is a compliance issue in itself.
  - Exposures include OAIC investigation, civil penalties, the newer statutory privacy tort, and customer contractual breach claims (possibly including Bluefen).
  - The Seller's "not material" view is unsupported by its own disclosure.
- **Push back:**
  - Request the incident timeline, logs, the forensic or investigation report, the NDB assessment, and any OAIC or customer notifications. Request privilege-appropriate access.
  - Require the Seller to complete the investigation, and make any required notifications, before Completion, in consultation with the Buyer.
  - Add a specific indemnity for all loss arising from the incident (regulatory, remediation, notification, customer claims, legal costs), outside the general limitations and backed by escrow or retention.
  - Add a warranty that the disclosed facts are complete and accurate, and that there are no other incidents.
  - Consider a MAC or termination right if the investigation reveals significant access.
  - Expect W&I insurers to exclude this known matter, so the indemnity must come from the Seller.

### 10. Sandbar supplier renewals (Medium)
- **Facts:** Three "related" renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 total). The Disclosure Letter says to read them together and says nothing on whether they are terminable, accrued or ordinary course. The Seller calls them ordinary-course costs.
- **Why it matters:**
  - Splitting one arrangement into three pieces of AUD 110,000 may keep each below a material-contract or interim-covenant threshold.
  - If "related" means related party (to Harbourglass or management), this may be leakage.
  - If they are prepaid or committed, they may be debt-like.
- **Push back:**
  - Get the contracts and confirm the counterparty relationship.
  - Aggregate related contracts when applying material-contract and conduct-of-business thresholds.
  - Require Buyer consent for renewals or commitments during the interim period.
  - If any are related-party, treat them as leakage subject to a pound-for-pound indemnity.
  - Treat any unpaid committed amounts not in the ordinary course as Debt.

### 11. Title evidence, DD-012 (Medium)
- **Issue:** Title rests solely on the Company's own share register. The Seller expressly disclaims that we have verified it.
- **Push back:**
  - Cross-check the register against the ASIC company extract and historical filings, the constitution, and the history of share issues and transfers.
  - Confirm there are no options, convertibles, ESOP entitlements or rights to issue shares.
  - Confirm there is no share security, particularly in favour of Riverlark.
  - Retain full fundamental title warranties: legal and beneficial ownership, free from Encumbrances, fully paid, no other rights. These should be supported by the item 1 treatment and the Riverlark releases.

### 12. Tax and IP "settled under the general regime" (Medium-High)
- **Issue:** The Seller seeks to put tax and IP inside the 20% cap and 18-month window.
- **Push back:**
  - Tax: a standalone pre-Completion tax indemnity and tax warranties, capped at 100% of the price. The claim period should cover the ATO amendment period plus a buffer (typically around 5–7 years), with no limit for fraud or evasion. Include conduct-of-claims provisions.
  - IP: a higher cap and a longer period, or treat IP as a fundamental-adjacent warranty, given the Ironquay chain-of-title gap.

### 13. Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) characterisations (Low-Medium)
- **Issue:** The Seller characterises these as a notification obligation only and as an assignment restriction that is not triggered by a share sale. Those are the Seller's readings.
- **Push back:**
  - Confirm independently against the full documents, looking in particular for "deemed assignment" or change-in-control definitions.
  - Make the notifications a Completion deliverable.
  - Make sure [1.4] does not convert the Seller's legal interpretation into a disclosure that defeats a warranty if that interpretation proves wrong.

### 14. General cap, thresholds and time limit (Medium: negotiable)
- **Cap of 20% (AUD 4.8m):** Within market range for general warranties. It is acceptable only if items 1, 2, 7, 8, 9 and 12 are carved out. If W&I insurance is used, adjust the structure: a Seller cap of around 1% for general warranties, with the insurer covering the rest, while specific indemnities stay with the Seller.
- **De minimis of AUD 25,000 (about 0.1%):** Broadly market. Allow related claims to be aggregated.
- **Basket of AUD 250,000 (about 1%), excess-only:** Push for a tipping basket, so recovery is from the first dollar once the threshold is crossed, or a lower threshold.
- **18 months:** Seek 24 months, so that at least two audit cycles fall within the window.

---

## Part B: Summary of recommendations

**Process**
1. Reject the [STANDARD] / [OPEN] categorisation in writing. All positions remain open.

**Limitations package**

2. Fundamental (title and capacity) warranties: 100% cap, 6–7 years, no thresholds, not qualified by disclosure.
3. Tax warranties and indemnity: standalone, 100% cap, ATO period plus buffer.
4. Carve out of all limitations: fraud, fundamental, tax, specific indemnities, leakage and price adjustment, equitable relief. Limitations to apply only to general Warranty Claims.
5. General warranties: accept around a 20% cap subject to the carve-outs. Seek a tipping basket and 24 months. Revisit if W&I is used.

**Disclosure and knowledge**

6. Delete general disclosure of the data room and public records. Allow only fair, specific disclosure. Delete or narrow [1.4].
7. Delete cl 8.3. Include express no-sandbagging-defence language.

**Conditions and Completion deliverables**

8. Bluefen: Buyer-waivable condition precedent; unconditional consent in an approved form with cl 11.3 conditions met; all reasonable endeavours; termination right; consider an escrow or retention for loss of the contract after Completion.
9. Riverlark: payout at Completion from the price; payout letter, deeds of release and PPSR releases as Completion deliverables; treated as Debt; specific indemnity.
10. Ironquay: SOW3 fees paid with evidence of cleared funds, plus a confirmatory IP assignment before Completion; broad specific indemnity outside the limitations.

**Price and funds flow**

11. DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420,000) plus PAYG, payroll tax, super and other on-costs: deducted as Debt or Transaction Costs, itemised in the funds flow, with a specific indemnity.
12. Sandbar: obtain the contracts; aggregate related contracts for thresholds; interim-period consent right; leakage or Debt treatment if related-party or committed outside the ordinary course.

**Risk items**

13. DD-006: urgent information request, including the NDB assessment status, since the 30-day window may have lapsed. Seller to complete the investigation and any notifications before Completion. Specific uncapped (or separately capped) indemnity backed by escrow. Completeness warranty. Consider a MAC or termination right.
14. Title: verify against ASIC records and the issue and transfer history. Confirm no share security or options. Full title warranties.
15. Lease and Mossvale: independently confirm there are no change-of-control triggers. Make notifications a Completion deliverable.

**Security for recovery**

16. Given the stacked known risks (Bluefen, DD-006, Ironquay), seek an escrow or retention of a portion of the price, for example 10% or AUD 2.4m, for around 18–24 months. Harbourglass is likely to distribute the sale proceeds, so a retention is the practical way to make sure indemnity claims can actually be paid.

These views should be checked by the NSW-qualified team against the full SPA draft and the underlying DD documents. In particular, I have not seen the full text of DD-002 cl 11.2–11.3, DD-003 cl 8.1 and 9.2, DD-007 or DD-009. If you share the incident timeline for DD-006, I can tighten the privacy analysis.
=== END ADVICE ===
